articles.title: Bleached corals thrive within days when touching healthy neighbour
articles.content: This video shows a bleached coral fragment brought back to health within weeks through fusion with a vibrant fragment from the same individual. Credit: Danny Collins Scientists have rapidly restored bleached coral in a laboratory by placing it in contact with a healthy fragment, giving hope for reversing widespread coral decline. Rising sea temperatures are stressing corals, causing the animals to expel the symbiotic algae that live in their tissues and give them their colour — a process known as bleaching. Because the photosynthetic algae (Symbiodiniaceae) provide corals with most of their nutrients, without them, the marine organisms are likely to starve and die. A team of researchers has now shown that it is possible to fully reverse this bleaching process, in just days. It reported the findings in Science Advances on 14 October 1 . “This incredible new result — that fast and full recovery is possible in bleached coral — can inspire solutions that eventually may be scalable,” says Fiorenza Micheli, a marine ecologist at Stanford University’s Center for Ocean Solutions in California and a co-author on the study. The healing touch In early 2025, marine scientist, and study co-author, Stephen Palumbi at Hopkins Marine Station in Pacific Grove, California, was working in the lab and noticed that two coral fragments in a tank were accidentally touching. Where the healthy and bleached fragment met, colour had begun to seep into the ghostly branch. “I’d never seen that before,” he remembers. Symbionts spread from the healthy into the bleached coral. Credit: Danny Collins Danny Collins, who was studying how disease spreads through coral contact as part of his PhD at Stanford, set out to investigate whether algae can also spread and, if so, how. He prepared ten pairs of coral fragments from the same animal ( Pocillopora damicornis )., Each pair had a bleached and a healthy fragment. He set up five pairs so that their fragments touched each other, and five with their fragments separated by a few millimetres. In the touching pairs, the bleached coral recovered within eight weeks. “We were blown away when we watched the colour of the algal symbionts transfer over to the bleached coral, reviving it in a very short period of time,” Collins says. By week two, the symbiont population was doubling every four days, which is much faster than the recovery times seen in studies of coral recovering naturally in the wild 2 , 3 . After touching the healthy fragment for a week, a bleached branch could fully recover on its own, even if separated from the healthy branch. In the slightly separated pairs, the bleached fragments died after 20 weeks. Using high-powered microscopy, the team showed that two coral fragments fuse together by creating a tissue bridge — enabling symbiont transfer. This only occurred for coral fragments taken from an individual of the same genetic make-up, called a genet. Fragments from different species and even different animals of the same spec

articles.title: Dam removals are bringing fish back across the northeastern United States
articles.content: Dam Removals Are Bringing Fish Back Across the Northeastern United States, Striking Down One Tiny Barrier at a Time While the demolition of big dams in the West gets more attention, many of these often-obsolete obstructions are also coming out of northeastern streams and rivers—and herring are returning in droves Dams block the flow of a river to hold water in a reservoir, which can be used for agriculture, recreation, household needs or industry. The flow of water through a dam can generate hydroelectric power. Aging dams are being dismantled across the country, restoring the natural flow to rivers. Jukka Jantunen / Shutterstock In 1859, a committee of farmers in Billerica, Massachusetts, having grown irked by a dam on the Concord River, hired a surveyor to justify its destruction. The dam, which powered a textile factory owned by an industrialist named Charles Talbot, was allegedly flooding their fields and spoiling their hay; now they wanted the wall and its reservoir gone. They hoped the surveyor’s evidence would persuade a court to order its obliteration. The surveyor—a conscientious, lushly bearded man of good repute—set about plumbing the Concord’s bottom, measuring its bridges and scrutinizing high-water marks. In truth, he didn’t love the work, describing surveying as “drudgery” in his journals. Henry David Thoreau ’s truest passion, of course, wasn’t surveying land, but writing about it. Aside from the paycheck, the now-legendary author had another motivation to take the Concord job: He despised the Talbot Mills Dam. A decade earlier, Thoreau had published the travelogue A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers , in which he inveighed against the dam for blocking the passage of spawning fish, especially American shad. “Poor shad! Where is thy redress?” Thoreau wrote . Although Thoreau’s surveys supported the farmers’ case, on appeal, the state of Massachusetts permitted the dam to remain. This can’t have surprised Thoreau, who knew that dams made for intractable opponents. “Perchance, after a few thousands of years, if the fishes will be patient, and pass their summers elsewhere meanwhile, nature will have leveled the Billerica dam,” he wrote. The Talbot Mills Dam in Billerica, Massachusetts—shown in this 1908 photograph—has vexed environmentalists, agrarians and native fish for centuries. Public domain via Billerica Public Library For many fish-blocking dams, however, it hasn’t taken “a few thousands of years” to level them after all. Since 1912, more than 2,300 dams have been purged from waterways in the United States, most in the last quarter-century. The dam-removal movement hit its apogee in 2024, when, by the accounting of the nonprofit American Rivers, dam removals reconnected more than 2,500 miles of once-fragmented waterways . The year’s biggest and best-publicized dam obliteration occurred on the Klamath River, where the dismantling of four aging hydroelectric dams opened more than 400 miles of spawning habitat in California
articles.summary: 美国东北部拆除大量老旧小水坝后，鲱鱼等鱼类重新洄游，河流生态逐步恢复。

articles.title: The Commodore 64 hardware simulator: break chips and pins, see the results
articles.content: c64-hw-sim simulates the motherboard of the Commodore 64, ASSY 250407, pin by pin. You can lift the leg of a chip, short it to ground or to +5V, pull a chip out of its socket, or open a resistor. Then you watch what the machine does: the picture on the monitor, the keyboard, every signal on the board. The program knows the board's netlist (the electrical connections on the PCB) and how each chip behaves at its pins. It knows nothing about what a broken Commodore 64 looks like: when you simulate a broken part and the screen fills with garbage, that garbage was computed from the circuit, not chosen by someone who knew what to expect. Here is an example. Lift pin 17 (A7) of the color RAM before power on, and the machine boots and looks healthy. The CPU writes and the VIC reads with the same wrong address, so the RAM simply aliases. Put the leg back, and the half of the color RAM that was never written shows up as random colors. Lift it again, and the screen is clean. A real 2114 does the same. With this program you can do mainly two things: Learn how the Commodore 64 works at a more intimate level, in a way that is hard to reproduce on real hardware without the risk of damaging it (and on most boards many chips are soldered, not socketed). If you have a broken C64 and some hypothesis about what could be broken, simulate it with this program and perhaps gain clues, so that you can desolder chips in the most logical order, and desolder as few of them as possible (desoldering is a boring process, and every time it risks damaging the board...). A matching symptom is a clue, not a proof: different faults can look the same, and the simulation has its limits (see below). Please note that even on fast computers this program struggles to simulate the C64 hardware at real speed. A real C64 is simulated at 31% of its speed on an Apple M3 Max, 39% on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 (Gorgon Halo), and 48% on an Apple M5 Max. This is not a problem for the goals of this program, but be warned: it is not an emulator to play games with. Above: the classic 10 PRINT CHR$(205.5+RND(1));:GOTO 10 maze is running when the character ROM (U5) is pulled out of its socket, and later put back. The CPU, the RAM and the program keep working; only the shapes of the characters are lost, as repairers know well. The scope is on the data line D0 of the ROM socket: with the socket empty, the bus floats (the dotted segments) whenever the VIC fetches a character shape. Shown at C64 speed. I (antirez) got the idea for this program while using and observing Andre Weissflog's (floooh) chips, emulators of the 6502, VIC-II, CIA, SID and friends that use pins as their interface. The next step was to take this approach, with his code as a starting point, to its logical extreme: pin-level models of every other part of the C64, the RAMs, the ROMs, the logic chips, the PLA, and so forth. The chip cores are floooh's chips, taken from c64-llm (zlib license). The board comes from bwack's C64-250407-Rep

articles.title: Gold is now the top U.S. export
articles.content: Image: AdobeStock Normally, America’s highest value exports are either oil, pharmaceuticals, or aircraft and their parts. Not now. Starting in October 2025, the value of gold exports has topped all other categories almost every month. For information on U.S. nonmonetary gold exports through December 2025, go to https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IEAXGG That’s not just because the price of gold reached record high prices. In February 2026, the tons of gold exported may have set an all-time record. The majority of gold exports are going to Switzerland, almost certainly to the refiners there. The second greatest quantity is going to Hong Kong, which is the global destination for gold going to China. The third greatest quantity of exported gold is going to the United Kingdom, where the London Bullion Market Association is the world’s largest gold trading exchange. The U.S. government is still reporting that its gold reserves are unchanged, so these exports look to be coming from current mine output and recycling operations. There is no official explanation of why U.S. gold exports have soared in recent months. But here is my speculation. There are multiple foreign governments growing leery of the future loss of purchasing power of the U.S. dollar, where they would prefer a different reserve asset with a better track record. Among all foreign central banks combined, the value of their gold reserves now exceeds their holdings of U.S. Treasury debt. Most foreign nations do not have the economic and financial power when negotiating with the U.S. government or businesses to demand payments for goods and services other than in dollars. China does have the economic and financial clout to press for payment in gold instead of dollars. The Chinese Central Bank has a track record the past few years of reducing its holdings of U.S. Treasury debt, from $1.096.1 trillion in April 2021 to $784.3 billion in February 2025, and the latest reported at just $693.3 billion in February 2026. Much of the decrease in Bank of China U.S. Treasuries has been replaced with gold. The Chinese government is also working to decrease the use of the dollar in international commerce, through the creation of alternative payment systems and the promotion of the “unit” for transactions among the member nations of the BRICS consortium. When you add up the gold held by the Chinese central bank (which has a decades-long track record of underreporting gold reserves, Chinese sovereign investment funds, the Chinese military, the inventories held by companies owned directly by the Chinese government or the Chinese military, and private citizenry, there are multiple analysts who consider that nation effectively controls the greatest amount of gold of any government. When you put these factors together, my suspicion is that a high percentage of U.S. gold exports are going to China, though some must first detour through Swiss refineries to convert the gold into kilogram bars of acceptable purity.

articles.title: You could have invented transformers from memory
articles.content: Retrieving a character from memory. The recall worsens as the number of memories grows. Large language models today can recall obscure facts from every corner of the world. Most recently, I was running late for a friend’s board game night, so I asked Astra to remind me the rules to Dune: Imperium. It gladly narrated them to me as I drove over and helped me remember the rules well enough for me to play again. We’re so used to asking models about anything that we take their vast knowledge for granted. How do models remember so much information? And how much can they store? In this post, I’ll go through an intuitive way to look at linear maps, MLPs, and self-attention as different kinds of memory stores. From this intuition we can derive some heuristics for how much memory each layer can store. The key property that characterizes a “good” memory store is its ability to recall what it stored. After all, even if we could store infinitely many facts, it’s not very helpful if we can’t recall them when we need to. The more memories we store, the more they interfere with each other when we try to recall one. So throughout the post we’ll focus on one quantity, the interference-to-signal ratio, which measures how much the other memories get in the way during recall. The number of memories a store can hold before the interference grows as large as the signal is its capacity . We’ll develop this perspective and show how you can go from a linear layer to something better, an MLP, which improves both capacity and recall, and then all the way to self-attention, which has very good recall and can store a potentially unbounded number of memories. With 64-dimensional keys, that’s a jump from about 64 memories, to about 2,700, to over a million. Here are the terms we’ll use throughout. A memory store is a function $f$ that holds $M$ memories, for $i = 1, \ldots, M$. A memory is one key-value pair: a key $k_i \in \reals^{d_k}$, used for lookup based on similarity, and a value $v_i \in \reals^{d_v}$, which is what we want to retrieve. To use $f$, we query it with an input $x$, and it recalls an output $f(x)$. A good memory store recalls $v_i$ when we query it with $k_i$, or with another vector similar to $k_i$. In the literature, a memory store that recalls by similarity is called an associative memory . An outer product memory store # The most basic memory store is linear: it simply accumulates memories via outer products, $$W = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i k_i\transpose = V\transpose K$$ where the rows of $K \in \reals^{M\times d_k}$ and $V \in \reals^{M\times d_v}$ are the keys $k_i\transpose$ and the values $v_i\transpose$. To store a new memory $(k, v)$, we simply add $vk\transpose$ to the existing weights. Aside: a gradient descent step writes a memory Take a linear layer $y = Wx$ inside a network with a scalar loss $L$, and let $\bar y = \grad L(y)$ be the gradient of the loss with respect to the layer’s output. The gradient with respect to $W$ is $\bar y x\transpose$, s

articles.title: The NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty Has Been Claimed
articles.content: We now know how the seeds of the NIST elliptic curves were generated: they’re not the hash of some saucy sentence, but the output of drand48 seeded with the time, which was indeed in 1997–98. John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis from Anthropic solved the riddle and on October 15th, 2026, at 01:07:51 UTC, claimed the full bounty I announced three years ago . They chose to donate the prize to ISRG , the non-profit that operates Let’s Encrypt, tripling its value to $36,864 (36 Ki$). Thank you to Amir Omidi, Chris Palmer, Colm MacCárthaigh, David Adrian, David Anderson, Jeff Hodges, Matt Green, Matthew McPherrin, Paul Kehrer, Ryan Sleevi, and Soatok for contributing to the bounty. This helps fill out a page of cryptographic history, and reinforces our confidence in these critical cryptographic primitives. The NIST elliptic curves (P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521) were published by NIST in FIPS 186-2 in 2000. They were generated at random according to ANSI X9.62 by taking an arbitrary seed, hashing it with SHA-1, and using the output to derive some of the parameters. Until this week, we had no idea how those arbitrary seeds were picked. The lore was that Dr. Jerry Solinas, who passed away in early 2023, generated them in 1997 by hashing some English sentences that he later forgot. You can read more in this article by Steve Weis or in the original bounty announcement . Turns out memory can play tricks on everyone: we now know they were instead generated with the POSIX-standard drand48 random number generator. The algorithm is as simple as passing the then-current UNIX timestamp to srand48() and then producing one byte at a time with drand48. Each sequence of 20 bytes is tried as a seed following ANSI X9.62 and rejected if the resulting curve is not valid. Some timestamps are used to generate multiple curves, by continuing to try seeds after accepting the first one. I reimplemented the algorithm in Go to verify the claim. Read more in Anthropic’s writeup . There are two additional undocumented criteria beyond the ANSI X9.62 ones, one fairly clear and one that still escapes us. If the bit length of the order n of the resulting curve is more than the bit length of the base field p of the curve, the seed is rejected. (The condition is not the stricter n < p , because prime239v2 has p < n < 2²³⁹.) This leaves us with roughly twice as many valid seeds as were published. We explored a number of explanations for this last bit, and found no good fit. Maybe the same RNG was used to validate seeds, consuming RNG output and skipping some potential candidates, although the “gaps” are not regular. Maybe there was just a bug in one of the algorithms that returned the wrong result half the time; these calculations, which we can now do with off-the-shelf software in minutes, were still very much state-of-the-art in 1997. srand48(863711343) [1997-05-15 15:49:03 +
articles.summary: 研究者查明NIST椭圆曲线种子由1997-98年时间戳播种的drand48生成，澄清长期悬而未决的密码学疑云。

articles.title: The Decoherence Trap: When AI slop drowns out the signal in an endless sea of noise
articles.content: TL;DR This essay introduces the concept of decoherence : the accumulation of locally valid but mutually incompatible or redundant models within a system, such that the cost of change is dominated by translating among those models and preventing unintended side-effects. Start ↙ ↘ ↙ ↘ Decoherent Coherent Step 600 Step 200 Start Step 200 Step 600 ← Decoherent ↔ Coherent → In other words, it's what happens when slop drowns out the signal in an endless sea of noise. Decoherence grows relative to the rate of change of a system, and it increases faster the more decoherent a system is, resulting in runaway exponential growth. It is not a new phenomenon, and humans have always countered it through carefully finding ways to do more with less, unifying disparate patterns and models into a cohesive whole. However, the widespread use of AI is currently producing it at a rate that is unsustainable. The good news is that this rules out the specter of runaway recursive self-improvement, the intelligence explosion that goes parabolic before anyone can react, as decoherence both prevents AI from improving in a bubble and limits the rate at which it can improve outside of it. The bad news is that we are barreling toward a different kind of disaster: Decoherence Collapse. Imagine a building, let's say a small office tower. When this building was built, they used a type of pipe that will degrade over time and eventually need to be replaced. This is standard infrastructural debt ; basic wear and tear, as they say. Then, let's say that when it comes time to replace the pipes, you need to change them over to a new standard. This could be because of new building code requirements, because the old pipes simply aren't made anymore, or because the new pipes are much better and easier to maintain. This is standard technical advancement debt , the need to upgrade and transition due to the forward progress of technology over time. There is a third form of debt that can arise based on how the transition from old pipes to new pipes is done. Consider the following options: Shut down the building and replace all of the pipes at once. This is a very disruptive and expensive method, since you can't use the building while the process is underway and you have to pay for the replacement up front. But the process is complete by the end of it. Shut down each floor, one at a time, and replace the pipes on that floor. This is less disruptive overall, but somewhat more expensive because you still have to pay up front, and you have to pay a premium for the extra labor required to keep things running smoothly as the work goes on. Replace the pipes as needed, when they begin to fail. This is the least disruptive strategy, and it allows you to amortize the cost of replacing all of the pipes over time, with one small repair after another. For most people, option 3 is very appealing. It allows them to keep things running smoothly and to spread out the cost of maintenance. And if we can just make

articles.title: The road to iroh 1.0
articles.content: It is done. After four years of work and various pivots we have released iroh 1.0. We have an expanding web site describing how iroh works under the hood, but we think it is important to also understand why we made the decisions that led to the current iroh. So here is a trip down memory lane / our commit history which highlights major turning points and design decisions. Perhaps more importantly, this post also covers some things we considered but ended up not doing . Iroh started as a rust implementation of ipfs . We got pretty far implementing various ipfs protocols and had interop with existing ipfs implementations working. Our goal with iroh was to target lightweight and resource constrained devices such as mobile phones. One area where we were unhappy with existing protocols was blob transfer. We started a working group within the ipfs community to come up with a new protocol, called the move the bytes working group . For that working group, we worked on a proposal for new blob transfer protocol. We wrote a small library called krakensync . Krakensync used BLAKE3 exclusively for content addressing because BLAKE3 supports verified incremental streaming of large blobs. After a few days we had a bare algorithm, and wanted to add networking to it to make the demo feel more real. We had only two days before the next meeting, and adding networking via rust-libp2p seemed impossible (Remember that this was before LLM coding assistants!). I had a tiny bit of previous experience with QUIC , and remembered from a project of a friend of mine, quinn-noise that quinn is both hackable and has a simple idiomatic rust API. So I tried to add networking via quinn and found it an absolute joy to work with. — Rüdiger In parallel to working on the ipfs compatible iroh, we worked on a side project to implement a single narrow real world use case: transfer of deltachat chat history when provisioning a new device. The technical task was to transfer a single large blob of backup data to a new device. There were hard constraints regarding disk and network usage. And the transfer had to be resumable. We found that we could not implement this very narrow use case with our ipfs based iroh implementation. Doing so would have had less than optimal network performance, and would have pulled in a very large dependency tree. So we started writing a lightweight sync library from scratch, using QUIC as the networking layer and BLAKE3 verified streaming for large blob transfer. Despite our best efforts, our main project was still far away from the theoretical limits. Meanwhile our sync side project showed what is possible. So we made the decision to no longer pursue the goal of staying compatible with existing ipfs implementations. Instead of multiaddrs , endpoints were identified by an Ed25519 public key. Instead of multihashes , we had BLAKE3. And instead of multiple transport protocols we had just QUIC. The new iroh was just QUIC based networking using quinn and blob transfe

articles.title: Why are we even doing all this?
articles.content: [This is a guest post by Rikab Gambhir . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] First, they came for the artists, and I did not speak out, because I was not an artist. Then, they came for the mathematicians, and I did not speak out, because I was not a mathematician. Then, they came for the physicists, and it was actually really cool and they gave me free tokens and promised to solve my entire field for me and now I can finally devote myself to the important work of publishing papers instead of doing physics In early October, OpenAI fulfilled every mathematician’s childhood dream. I am not a mathematician myself (merely a theoretical particle physicist, which some argue barely counts as a scientist either), so I can’t 100% say for certain what inspires someone to pursue mathematics. But, I imagine this dream is common to all academics: Looking up at the stars in wonderment, or enjoying a complex puzzle game, or being inspired by an encouraging teacher, and dreaming that one day an unfeeling corporate robot[1] will burn a rainforest to compile a list of 700 highly obscure barely-readable facts that *might* be true that nobody can understand as part of a marketing gimmick to raise hype for an IPO[2] . This is probably why most of you reading this got into academia. At least, that’s why I did. In 1941, Jorge Luis Borges imagined a library containing every possible book that could ever be written. Somewhere in this Library of Babel is a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the complete all-orders theory of quantum gravity, and all the papers I will ever write. Of course, there are also incorrect proofs, theories, and misleading Lean certificates , but that is besides the point. By the research standards of 2026, Borges’s Library of Babel would be the most successful research institution in human history, containing an inconceivably large number of potentially correct mathematical and physical results, blowing OpenAI’s mere 722 write-ups and even the physics community’s recent 2500 write-ups out of the water. Of course, most recognize that Borges was a visionless fool who failed to recognize the commercial potential of his library, as he never actually built it. He did not have the entrepreneurial STEM-spirit to raise venture capital, launch an IPO, and announce that he had the potential to solve all of mathematics. He was too concerned about the futility of sorting through randomized slop trying to understand what is correct and what isn’t and how to understand it all. But what did Borges know? He was only a writer, and we have already established that artists are obsolete. Fortunately, OpenAI has brought us one step closer to realizing Borges’s vision. Rather than generating every possible mathematical paper, they’ve found a way to probabilistically generate things that look correct. An important aspect of this increase in efficiency is outsourcing the tedious, unprestigious, and unprofitable work o

articles.title: Making a 88x31 button book using ImageMagick
articles.content: Homepage Last edit: 16 Nov 2024 Making an 88x31 book-button using ImageMagick (On a posix system) Introduction If you've spent a considerable amount of time surfing the internet (and especially the Small Web), you might have seen an 88x31 button, or a few dozen of them. Some of them look like this: However, the nice thing about computer displays is that they are able to cope with quickly changing visuals, hence some have animation: I have noticed that among very numerous examples , i haven't seen any that'd go very far in that axis. Usually the animations are there just to catch your eye, or to display several words in succession. But why not Moby Dick? Size limitations I was surprised to find that there seems to be no limit to the number of frames in a GIF file, and that the maximum resolution is 2^16 by 2^16, which is 4295 megapixels. We are of course limiting ourselves to just 88 by 31 pixels (or 0.003 megapixel), which might mean that regular text fonts don't get much space to shine — Arial, for example, seems to become legible at a minimum of 10 pixels height, which allows us to display about eleven words at once. Alternative fonts As is often the case in computing, popular conventions end up upsetting someone enough that they develop an alternative way. In this case the alternative we're looking for are fonts designed to be legible at extremely low font sizes. There are some as small as 3x3, but personally I find TomThumb to be the golden middle here. You can get TomThumb in truetype here . Getting Moby Dick Firstly, you will want to obtain a plain text copy of the book's content. The methods might vary depending on what formats you have access to — you can use OCR to grab the text from a physical book , with an .EPUB or .PDF you can convert them (or even copy text manually), or you might get lucky and find what you're looking already shipped as a plain text .txt file, as is the case with Moby Dick . I downloaded the file and stripped the license at the start and the end. I also cropped off everything before the first chapter. Formatting the work If we take our button, which is 88x31, and our font, which is 6x4 (5x3 + spacing), we find that we can fit 5 rows of 22 characters each. ImageMagick, the tool we're going to use, is not very good at laying out text, so it'd be wise to take care of that ourselves. There's several ways to do this, but the neatest one uses three posix tools: cat, tr and fold: cat input.txt | tr '\n' ' ' | tr -d '\r' | fold -s -w 22 > 22w.txt cat is used to send the text to tr. tr translates each newline into a space, condensing the whole text file into one line. fold then takes that one line, splits it into multiple lines that are up to 22 characters wide (-w 22), and tries to avoid splitting words in half (-s). It's likely that at this point, your text looks fine. Mine was a bit garbled up, because fold doesn't handle multibyte characters well. I checked what non-ascii characters input.txt contained, and got rid of t

articles.title: Linus Torvalds on AI-assisted kernel contributions
articles.content: Loading... You are seeing this because the administrator of this website has set up Anubis to protect the server against the scourge of AI companies aggressively scraping websites. This can and does cause downtime for the websites, which makes their resources inaccessible for everyone. Anubis is a compromise. Anubis uses a Proof-of-Work scheme in the vein of Hashcash, a proposed proof-of-work scheme for reducing email spam. The idea is that at individual scales the additional load is ignorable, but at mass scraper levels it adds up and makes scraping much more expensive. Ultimately, this is a placeholder solution so that more time can be spent on fingerprinting and identifying headless browsers (EG: via how they do font rendering) so that the challenge proof of work page doesn't need to be presented to users that are much more likely to be legitimate. Please note that Anubis requires the use of modern JavaScript features that plugins like JShelter will disable. Please disable JShelter or other such plugins for this domain.

articles.title: Introducing GNOME OS Preview
articles.content: It’s been two years since my initial post about making GNOME OS an end-user general purpose OS. Today, we’re excited to announce that we’ve hit a major milestone! TL;DR: We’re launching a new edition called “GNOME OS Preview”, which is built from the latest stable GNOME release. This means that GNOME OS is no longer just a nightly OS for GNOME developers and testers! The Road to Stable Even though GNOME OS has been usable on real hardware for a few years now, its appeal was limited. We’ve only had the Nightly edition, which is constantly rebuilt to ship the latest git commit of every GNOME component (and a few others, like systemd and Flatpak). This form of GNOME OS is extremely useful, since GNOME developers and designers can daily-drive it to test the latest changes. However, it’s not something we’d recommend to non-developers. Over the past year, we’ve seen a lot of adoption of GNOME OS Nightly amongst GNOME developers, especially following the success of last year’s Summer of GNOME OS challenge. This has led to a significant uptick in contributions and initiatives aimed at improving user and developer experience. For instance: Thanks to Jonas Dreßler’s, Valentin David’s, and Sebastian Wick’s zswap enablement efforts, GNOME OS now handles devices with limited amounts of RAM without OOM stalls. Jonas also found a hack that lets GNOME OS dynamically grow the usable on-disk swap space on-demand, which makes zswap perform significantly better than usual. The recently released Test Center app allows you to install CI builds of Flatpak apps from a merge request, making it super easy to test experimental changes before they are even merged. On GNOME OS Nightly, Test Center can do the same with system components by applying them as a system extension. Jordan Petridis’s new Toolpak project aims to provide a clean solution for distributing and installing command-line applications that developers need in a cross-distro fashion, similarly to how Flatpak and Flathub work for graphical apps. Of course, long-term our goal is an OS for the broader public. We’re working on this across a number of different fronts, including: Enablement for systemd-homed across the stack, allowing for stronger per-user disk encryption and other benefits. Experimental work in the kernel to solve a bunch of limitations we’ve run into with filesystems. Ada Magicat went on a deep dive on her recent All Systems Go talk ! Deep integration between systemd-homed and the session’s keyring, to increase security of the session’s lock screen. Dhanuka Warusadura gave a lightning talk at All Systems Go about his work on this. A new feature-complete installer, to replace the current placeholder installer. Julian Sparber also gave a talk about this at All Systems Go , with a live demo! Support for delta updates in systemd-sysupdate , to avoid downloading a full 2 GB image every time. Better integration with the TPM, including a graphical TPM recovery UI. Currently, trying to type a TPM recover
articles.summary: GNOME团队宣布推出基于最新稳定版的GNOME OS Preview，标志其向通用终端操作系统迈出重要一步。

articles.title: Interactive refactoring in gopls
articles.content: When editing code in a modern IDE or editor, developers rely on its refactoring features to automate common transformations. Today, we are excited to introduce interactive refactoring in gopls , powered by a new capability we are proposing for the Language Server Protocol (LSP) that brings dynamic, multi-step dialogs directly into your favorite editor. Crucially, we designed this capability (in collaboration with the Dart team) not just for Go, but as an open standard for all programming languages and editor ecosystems. Working support is already available in gopls v0.24.0 and the official Go extension for VS Code v0.56.0. What is the Language Server Protocol (LSP)? The LSP is an open standard that decouples language-specific features from specific text editors. As you navigate and edit code, your editor (such as VS Code, Neovim, or Emacs) and a language server (like gopls) engage in a continuous JSON-RPC exchange to provide features like autocomplete, hover documentation, diagnostics, and code actions. Multi-step code transformation Today, almost every code transformation in the LSP is like a function of no parameters: you trigger the operation, and the server immediately computes the edits. (Renaming a symbol is the sole exception: because it is a function of one parameter, the desired new name, it required its own dedicated PrepareRename RPC in the protocol.) "Add struct tags", without questions The language server must deduce the user’s intent from context alone, namely the cursor position and the enclosing syntax tree. When that context is not enough, the server is forced into one of two choices: apply a one-size-fits-all default, or refrain from offering the transformation altogether. The limitation lies not in gopls’s ability to compute the necessary edits, but in the LSP’s lack of a mechanism for language servers to ask the user for input. For many transformations, this parameterless model works well. But many others need additional input from the user: which struct tags to add and in what naming convention, which interface to implement, which file to move a declaration to. Without a way to ask, gopls could only guess—“Add struct tags”, for example, always produced json tags in camelCase —or not offer the refactoring at all. With interactive refactoring, language servers can now easily provide new operations with one or more parameters. "Add struct tags", with questions While some language extensions have worked around this limitation by embedding custom, language-specific dialog logic directly into individual editors, doing so leaves behind other editors (such as Neovim and Emacs) that stick strictly to the LSP with minimal custom client code. More importantly, editor-specific workarounds go against the fundamental purpose of the LSP: to decouple language-specific features from editors so that each server improvement benefits every client. Our LSP interactive refactoring proposal ( microsoft/language-server-protocol#1164 ) solves this by
articles.summary: gopls引入交互式重构功能，基于LSP新提案能力，让Go开发者在编辑器中实现动态代码变换。

articles.title: Intuitive concurrent programming in any language
articles.content: Build predictable , concurrent , time-sensitive , and distributed systems. Lingua Franca is a coordination language for efficient, deterministic, multi-threaded, time-sensitive, embedded, and distributed programs. The result of decades of research, it offers more repeatable behavior than other concurrent programming frameworks, including threads, pub-sub, actors, and service-oriented architectures. Get Started Read the Docs Deterministic Concurrency Lingua Franca offers a straightforward way to write deterministic multi-threaded and distributed applications, eliminating concerns about thread management, synchronization, and race conditions. Built-in Timing Semantics Timing is embedded within Lingua Franca's core, empowering developers to handle time-sensitive tasks with precision and without the complex timing logic typically required in concurrent programming. Simplified Distribution Lingua Franca enables seamless transition from single to distributed system architectures with minimal modifications, abstracting away the complexities of distributed systems programming. Architect your application in LF import Player from "../Player.lf" main reactor RockPaperScissors { // Instantiate two Player reactors here player1 = new Player (id = 1 ) player2 = new Player (id = 2 ) // Make connections between them player2 . reveal -> player1 . observe player1 . reveal -> player2 . observe } Lingua Franca Diagram for the RockPaperScissor Program R o c k P a p e r S c i s s o r s p l a y e r 2 : P l a y e r o b s e r v e r e v e a l p l a y e r 1 : P l a y e r o b s e r v e r e v e a l A New Programming Paradigm Lingua Franca is the first reactor-oriented coordination language. It allows you to specify reactive components and compose them. Lingua Franca eliminates race conditions by construction, makes it easy to specify timed behavior, and removes the need to perform manual synchronization. Consider a game of "rock paper scissors" where two players need to reveal their choice simultaneously. In Lingua Franca, "at the same time" has a clear and precise meaning. This makes the implementation simple and intuitive, and guarantees it to be fair. If the Player class were to observe the other's choice before revealing its own, Lingua Franca's causality analysis would find a causality loop and tell you that the program is invalid. Not a New Programming Language With Lingua Franca, you forget about thread libraries or message passing middlewares, but you continue using the languages you like. The bodies of reactive code that make up the functionality of reactors are written in the programming language of your choice. We currently support C, C++, Python, TypeScript, and Rust. Open-source and Supported by Research Lingua Franca was first developed at UC Berkeley where it was influenced by decades worth of research in models of computation. A world map showing where key Lingua Franca contributors reside. A world map showing where key Lingua Franca contributors reside. Short

articles.title: android/skills (Kotlin)
articles.content: Android skills are a dedicated repository of AI-optimized, modular instructions and resources, to help agents better understand and execute specific patterns that follow the best practices and guidance on Android development from developer.android.com . Android skills follow the open-standard agent skills - markdown files (SKILL.md) that provide a technical specification of a task, and ground LLMs with information on specialized domains and workflows. Our Android skill development focuses on use cases and workflows where evaluations show LLMs underperform . We aren't prioritizing well-established areas where LLMs are already proficient, such as basic Jetpack Compose best practices. To learn more, read the official documentation: Use Android CLI to install a specific skill into the current directory: android skills add r8-analyzer --project=. Use Android CLI to install all Android skills to directories for all detected agents: If you don't have any existing agent directories and don't specify particular agents, the skills will be installed for Gemini and Antigravity at ~/.gemini/antigravity/skills . Options: --all - Add all Android skills. If omitted, only the android-cli skill will be installed. --agent - A comma-separated list of agents to install the skill for. If omitted, the skill will be installed for all detected agents. --project - Path to a project root in which to install the skills. To update all skills or specific ones, run: android skills update --all android skills update wear-compose-m3 Install as an agent plugin Claude Code : /plugin install android-skills --marketplace android/skills Codex: codex plugin marketplace add android/skills codex plugin add android-skills@android-skills Your agent automatically activates skills that are relevant to your task. To use a skill, prompt your agent to complete a task that is related to the skill, for example "Make my app UI edge-to-edge." The agent should automatically find and use the skill if it has been installed. AI can make mistakes, so always double-check the results. Submit a GitHub issue to provide feedback, report issues, or make new skill requests and changes. Public contributions are not accepted at this time. Android Skills is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 . See the LICENSE.txt file for details. Review our community guidelines This project follows Google's Open Source Community Guidelines .

articles.title: Bug turns one of the biggest fears about Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses into reality
articles.content: Some Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses were recording people’s conversations without the wearer knowing. The recordings occurred without users saying the prompt phrase (“Hey, Meta”), in a bug that Meta says has been fixed. This week, some users reported online that their Ray-Ban Metas were recording without their consent. A person going by Kindly-Audience-137 on Reddit, for example, said this happened to them across three Meta Ray-Bans and that they had the “Respond without Hey Meta” setting turned off. The person said the Meta AI app “saves audio recordings and text transcripts of these conversations in my conversation history.” “I believe this deserves a serious technical investigation. Customers should not have to wonder whether their private conversations are being captured when they have not intentionally activated their glasses’ AI assistant,” the Reddit user said. Android Authority reported the discussions on Tuesday. Later that day it published a response from Meta that read: “This issue has been resolved. People can manage, review, and delete voice logs of their interactions with Meta AI via settings at any time.” Although Meta’s brief message suggests that the bug is fixed, the broader privacy problem remains. Unanswered questions Meta hasn’t said what caused the Ray-Ban Metas to record people without user consent. Reddit user Kindly-Audience-137 said they “first noticed this behavior after a recent firmware update,” but Meta hasn’t confirmed if a faulty update caused the bug. We also don’t know how many Meta smart glasses were affected. There are a few reports online, but Android Authority said it was unable to replicate the problem before Meta said it fixed it. Ars Technica sent Meta a message asking what it’s doing to prevent future bugs like this from happening again and how many devices were affected. We’ll update this article if we hear back. Even a handful of affected devices is cause for concern, though. Before reports of this bug, privacy advocates had already expressed widespread concerns about Meta’s smart glasses, as well as those from other vendors. Beyond the fear that naturally accompanies the release of new technology that features a microphone and camera, Meta’s glasses pushed the boundaries of privacy further with their more inconspicuous look, prompting concern about how easy it could be for someone to secretly record another person. Meta has previously tried to assuage concerns by pointing to the fact that its glasses light up when recording audio or video. But the bug this week shows that even with this light activated, it’s possible for the smart glasses to record inadvertently. Meta’s brief statement does little to alleviate those worries. Meanwhile, the bug lends some credence to reports and trepidation that Ray-Ban Metas are creating recordings without subjects’ knowledge. Fears brought to life Meta has been steadfast in its push for gadgets that put microphones and cameras in people’s homes and on their faces , while
articles.summary: 部分Ray-Ban Meta智能眼镜在用户不知情下未经唤醒词即录制对话，Meta称漏洞已修复。

articles.content: Google researchers open sourced EnvHarness, a framework that dynamically adapts agent-training environments to an agent's weaknesses without modifying the agent, environment, or evaluation system. According to the researchers, this approach can improve both learning effectiveness and efficiency while helping agents overcome their weaknesses. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: 谷歌开源 EnvHarness 框架，可动态调整代理训练环境以针对其弱点，提升学习效果与效率。

articles.title: Zod Brings In-Process Schema Compilation and a 9x Cut in Memory Footprint
articles.content: Zod is a TypeScript-focused schema validation library that recently released versions 4.5 and 4.6. Key updates include schema compilation for faster data parsing, significant memory usage reductions, and new validation features. The library supports efficient validation processes and remains popular in the JavaScript ecosystem, achieving millions of downloads weekly. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: TypeScript 校验库 Zod 发布 4.5/4.6 版，引入进程内模式编译，内存占用降低约 9 倍并新增校验特性。

articles.title: Uber Automates Dependency Analysis Across Its Service Mesh
articles.content: Uber has developed an automated dependency analysis system that uses RPC middleware and production metrics to correlate caller and downstream failures. The approach classifies dependencies as fail-close, fail-open, or unknown and addresses limitations of sampled distributed tracing for rare failures across Uber’s large service mesh. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: Uber 构建自动化依赖分析系统，利用 RPC 中间件与生产指标关联调用方与下游故障，弥补采样追踪不足。

articles.title: AI in Production: Panellists Highlight Silent Failures, Harness Engineering, and Agent Governance
articles.content: A recent InfoQ webinar examined operational challenges in deploying agentic systems. Key points included issues like semantic and embedding drift, which can lead to significant errors. Experts discussed the need for automated code reviews, continuous evaluation of models, and enhanced privacy measures. The session emphasised a strategic approach to deployment and security management. By Olimpiu Pop
articles.summary: InfoQ 网络研讨会探讨代理系统生产落地难题，包括语义漂移、静默失败、自动代码审查与代理治理。

articles.title: Grafana Applies SLOs and Error Budgets to AI Agent Behaviour
articles.content: Grafana Labs is proposing a familiar reliability engineering approach for one of the less familiar problems in modern software: how to measure whether an AI agent is actually behaving well. By Craig Risi
articles.summary: Grafana Labs 提出用 SLO 与错误预算衡量 AI 代理行为表现，把可靠性工程方法引入代理评估。

articles.title: Mini book: Evolutionary Architecture in Practice
articles.content: Discover how to keep software evolvable as systems, technology, and teams shift. This edition explores agentic fitness functions for semantic drift, treating human comprehension as a core design metric, cross-cloud guardrails for regional autonomy, and aligning technical boundaries with Conway’s Law. Move beyond static diagrams to continuous feedback systems that keep change safe and intentional. By InfoQ
articles.summary: InfoQ 迷你书探讨演进式架构实践，涵盖语义漂移适应函数、人类理解度指标与跨云护栏等主题。

articles.title: Helidon 27 Introduces Restructured Programming Models and New Messaging and Data Modules
articles.content: The release of Helidon 27 is the first release that follows the Oracle Tip & Tail Model of Library Development by which the Tip adopts the latest Java technology while the Tail provides a more stable and secure baseline. Concurrent with the release of JDK 27, new features in Helidon 27 include: an introduction to new major modules, Helidon Messaging and Helidon Data JDBC. By Michael Redlich
articles.summary: Helidon 27 发布，采用 Oracle Tip & Tail 模式，重构编程模型并新增消息与数据模块，同步 JDK 27。

articles.title: Presentation: Exploding GPUs
articles.content: Andrew Martin discusses why AI security is fundamentally tied to Kubernetes security. He shares insights into the evolving AI threat landscape, covering non-deterministic agent behavior, GPU supply chain vulnerabilities, shared compute risks, and practical defense strategies - from prompt firewalling to agentic identity - to help secure cloud-native AI workloads in production environments. By Andrew Martin
articles.summary: 演讲指出 AI 安全本质上是 Kubernetes 安全，剖析代理非确定性、GPU 供应链风险及提示防火墙等防御策略。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 报道中期选举 AI 生成广告支出超 1.37 亿美元，约七成未标注 AI，引发透明度担忧。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 汇总：Anthropic 警告小型 AI 模型或将能自我复制到智能家电，另有大型研究等热点。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第536期汇总专家分享，聚焦AI能否自主做研究、治理话语权、军事规划应用及进入个人电脑等前沿议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第535期指出企业因AI成本过高转向更便宜模型，大规模部署进入日常使用，同时AI受限或撤除的场景增多。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第534期报道高校IT负责人首次将AI列为首要任务，剑桥拒Turnitin新条款，达特茅斯调查教务长写作，AI使用已非未来议题。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: AI Weekly第533期揭示Meta AI电话代理背后由人工接线员接手，自动化与隐私边界中的隐藏人工介入变得可见。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第531期指出AI实验室在未就故障报告达成一致前便发布代理，隐私泄露、模型自写记忆与监管问题浮现。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #530: Applied AI This Week
articles.content: Companies are giving AI specific jobs: checking security cameras, helping farmers understand their records, searching satellite images, and preparing sales quotes. This edition explains how those tools work, who can use them, and what companies have reported so far.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第530期介绍企业将AI用于安防监控、农业记录、卫星图像搜索和销售报价等具体岗位，并说明使用方式与反馈。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #529: OpenAI faces 50-plus lawsuits over alleged ChatGPT harm
articles.content: Thirty new complaints come from survivors of a Canadian school shooting. They accuse OpenAI of failing to warn police; the company disputes key claims.
articles.summary: OpenAI因ChatGPT涉嫌伤害面临50多起诉讼，其中30起来自加拿大校园枪击案幸存者，指控其未警告警方，公司否认关键指控。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #528: What are companies building with AI? An Applied AI Deep Dive
articles.content: We went looking for what companies are actually building with AI. The answer was not more chatbots. It was drones carrying diagnostic samples, driverless Frito-Lay trucks, AI-guided flight paths, repair copilots, and rugged GPU laptops in Ukraine. We reviewed 136 use cases from the last 20 days. The biggest surprise: only 38 included a reported outcome.
articles.summary: AI Weekly第528期深挖企业实际AI应用，发现重点并非聊天机器人，而是诊断无人机、无人卡车、飞行路径与维修助手等136个用例。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw作者Gavriel Cohen讲述40小时周末项目如何成为爆红开源项目，并因安全顾虑打造容器隔离的OpenAI替代方案，进而创立企业AI公司。

articles.title: Changelog IRL @ PlanetScale (Sept 17, 2026)
articles.content: Changelog is taking over PlanetScale's HQ We’re getting together IRL!! On Thursday, September 17th, Changelog is taking over PlanetScale’s HQ in San Francisco for an evening of short talks and conversations about AI, developer tools and what people are building. We’ll have a few conversations with special guests and time for questions, food, drinks and hanging out. I’ll be joined by three builders pushing this idea forward, starting with Dan Robinson from Detail (detail.dev), with more guests to be announced very soon. I also have 80 limited edition t-shirts printed to give away! This won’t be a few presentations followed by everyone heading home. We’re doing this Changelog-style: live conversations, questions from the room, drinks, and plenty of time afterward for the hallway track. If you’re in San Francisco, register to come hang out! Changelog IRL Thursday, September 17th, 2026 6:00pm – 9:00pm PDT PlanetScale HQ 108 Natoma St, San Francisco, CA 94105 Speakers Dan Robinson, (Detail) Christian Glassiognon, Developer Educator at PlanetScale TBD Schedule 6:00 - 6:45pm: Doors open, food, drinks and networking 6:45 - 7:00pm: Welcome and opening chat with Adam 7:00 - 8:00pm: Changelog IRL with Dan and special guests 8:00 - 8:15pm: Questions 8:30 - 9:00pm: Hanging out and networking 9:00pm: Close All times Pacific. PlanetScale HQ, 108 Natoma St, San Francisco.
articles.summary: Changelog 将于2026年9月17日在旧金山 PlanetScale 总部举办线下活动，围绕 AI、开发工具及开发者实践展开短演讲与交流。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com 联合创始人 Peer Richelsen 在播客中提出多数开源仓库可能已被攻陷，并讨论 AI 如何改变知识获取与开源生态。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale 推出5美元 Postgres 服务，CEO Sam Lambert 介绍 Vitess 重写、AI 代理部署变更及500TB表秒级回滚等能力。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst 创始人 Haroon Meer 介绍 Canary 蜜罐与数字绊线，用于检测攻击者触碰 AWS API 密钥等内部资源的行为。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: Max Stoiber 讲述从 react-boilerplate、styled-components 等开源项目到加入 OpenAI 负责 ChatGPT 插件目录与平台。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.
articles.summary: Cloudflare 的 Matt Carey 介绍 Code Mode，让单个 MCP 服务器以约1000 token 上下文暴露全部约2500个 API 端点。

articles.title: Automation at the speed of Swamp
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Adam Jacob, founder of System Initiative and creator of Swamp, about what happens when AI agents change the entire shape of software development. We discuss how he went from an 18-person team down to five and shipped Swamp 900 times in four weeks, why he brought User Acceptance Testing (UAT) testing back from the 90s, why software architecture (and domain-driven design) suddenly matters more than knowing how to write code, the live demo where I pointed Swamp at my Proxmox box and watched it write its own automation (blew my mind!!), and why he'll never accept a pull request to Swamp, ever.
articles.summary: System Initiative 创始人 Adam Jacob 讲述团队从18人缩减至5人，四周内发布 Swamp 900次，AI 代理重塑软件开发流程。

articles.title: Bitwarden CLI compromised
articles.content: Bitwarden's CLI got hit by the Checkmarx supply-chain campaign, TypeScript 7.0 beta lands with the Go-rewritten compiler running ~10x faster than 6.0, and pgBackRest lost its maintainer of thirteen years leaving anyone running production Postgres with a real dependency-trust task this week. We've also got Ubuntu 26.04 LTS shipping with TPM-backed full-disk encryption, and Matz dropping Spinel as an AOT path that takes Ruby to native binaries. This week was a good reminder that the tools we depend on are all moving at once. Security, performance, and maintenance aren't isolated threads.
articles.summary: Bitwarden CLI 遭 Checkmarx 供应链攻击，TypeScript 7.0 beta 编译器提速约10倍，pgBackRest 维护者离职引发依赖信任问题。

articles.title: Exploring with agents
articles.content: Today on the show I’m talking with Amelia Wattenberger — designer, data-viz veteran, ex-GitHub Next, and now designing Intent at Augment Code. What if the last 30% of any software project is about to become the hardest part you’ve ever done? That’s the argument Amelia is making today. We discuss the identity crisis developers are having as agents take over the keyboard, the epic redesign of developer tooling in this agent-first world, the arc from autocomplete to chat to CLI back to UI, why Intent treats a workspace as their core primitive not a chat thread, the tradeoffs between one-worktree-per-agent vs. one-worktree-per-task, and why she thinks prototyping just got easier but finishing got harder.
articles.summary: 设计师 Amelia Wattenberger 讨论 AI 代理如何改变探索式开发，认为软件项目最后30%的工作将变得异常艰难。

articles.title: Does a Universal Basic Income Bring Long-Term Changes?
articles.content: For more than a year, The New York Times followed recipients of a universal basic income program who received $1,330 a month for an entire year. There were benefits, but also the everyday challenges of being poor, and turning their life around "did not turn out to be quite that simple." Across Silicon Valley, experimental guaranteed income programs have quietly taken off. Google began funding six different initiatives in 2022 as part of a $50 million donation to nonprofits in the San Francisco Bay Area, saying basic income could be a novel way to prevent homelessness in one of the nation's most expensive locations. Each program has hundreds of participants who receive around $1,000 a month, and academics study the results. State and federal tax laws limit the lengths of the programs and the payment amounts. The studies have found that most basic income programs improve short-term employment and mental health while reducing food insecurity. But while data from these efforts has been closely tracked, less is known about the individual journeys of participants... The Times ultimately shadowed three people... All of the program participants, including the ones The Times followed, were previously homeless and transitioning off a housing stipend that paid for a portion of their rent, and many received the payments on top of other social assistance like food stamps. The Times's findings mirrored the academic studies. For all three recipients, the instant benefits of basic income were clear: They had breathing room for groceries, rent and other expenses. But the success of the payments in another area — giving people more free time and opportunity in the long term — was mixed. "It's a lot to ask of someone to get their life together in 12 months, when a lot of these issues are structural or systemic," said Jennifer Loving, who runs Destination: Home, a nonprofit that administers basic income programs in Silicon Valley. "And the world around them isn't getting cheaper." One
articles.summary: 纽约时报追踪一年每月领取1330美元的无条件基本收入项目，发现虽有收益，但受助者生活改善并不简单。

articles.title: Court Agrees with EFF: Utah's VPN Law Demands a Technical Impossibility
articles.content: "When state lawmakers attempt to rewrite how the internet works," argues an EFF blog post, "users rely on courts to recognize that laws can't make technical impossibilities a reality." "That's why we were happy to see that a court has blocked Utah's attempt to outlaw the privacy protections of Virtual Private Networks (VPNs)." In a win for digital rights, a federal judge has issued a preliminary injunction blocking Utah's SB 73, the state's draconian anti-VPN age verification law... Signed into law earlier this year, SB 73 attempted to regulate adult websites by requiring them to block VPN users or to identify the physical location of visitors using them or similar tools that mask their network traffic. It even went so far as to prohibit websites from offering instructions on how to use a VPN to bypass these checks. This made Utah, to EFF's knowledge, the first state in the nation to target the use of VPNs to avoid legally mandated age-verification gates. The Utah federal court halted enforcement of the law's VPN provisions last week, ruling that the law likely violates the U.S. Constitution's prohibition on passing laws that significantly burden businesses and people outside Utah's borders. SB 73 burdens the rights of all internet users outside of Utah because it requires adult websites to either know every visiting user's physical location, and then block those in Utah, or to verify every visitor's age just in case they might be in Utah. The law's "actual-location provision in practice requires an entity to perform age verification services for every user visiting its site from any location because the entity would violate the law if even one of those users happened to be obfuscating," the court wrote. The court essentially ruled that Utah has less-burdensome ways to prevent Utah minors from accessing adult websites than requiring all users in the world to comply with SB 73. EFF's position is that "forcing platforms to detect and block privacy-preserving tools und
articles.summary: 法院支持 EFF 观点，裁定犹他州要求 VPN 屏蔽特定内容的法案在技术上不可行，并予以阻止。

articles.title: MapQuest Shows Location of Flock (and Other ALPR) Cameras
articles.content: MapQuest creates a new layer (that can be toggled on and off), Gizmodo reports: After promising not to comply with the Trump administration's "Lake America" gimmick, the platform announced a new "Surveillance Layer" that displays the locations of automated license plate readers (ALPRs), including those from Flock Safety. Per MapQuest, its new tool will identify the locations of known outdoor surveillance cameras and plate readers from Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia, Verkada, and others. While the company didn't specify how it sources its data, it appears to be similar to the data amassed by DeFlock, which maintains a user-submitted map of ALPR camera locations. MapQuest may be sourcing the information from DeFlock and the OpenStreetMap project. Engadget notes that MapQuest also recently added "useful, long-overdue features like Android Auto support and public transit directions." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: MapQuest 新增可开关的监控图层，显示自动车牌识别摄像头位置，包括 Flock 等厂商设备。

articles.title: Blue Origin Announces $330M Upgrades to Rocket Facilities for 'Multiple Flights Per Week'
articles.content: "Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin said Friday it plans to make extensive upgrades to its Florida launch facilities," reports CNBC, "with the goal of supporting multiple flights per week by the end of the decade." "The company will add two more launch and landing pads for New Glenn, its heavy-lift, partially reusable rocket." A $330 million expansion to its Rocket Park campus in Cape Canaveral, expected to be complete in the summer of 2027, will enable it to produce up to 150 upper stages of its New Glenn rocket annually, Blue Origin said in a blog post. "These investments are centered on one goal: building the capacity to support more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently," Ian Richardson, Blue Origin's senior vice president of operations, wrote in the post. "As we look ahead, this infrastructure is designed to support multiple flights per week by the end of the decade...." Blue Origin said it's building a new customer integration facility with the U.S. Space Force at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station that will enable it to "prepare multiple missions at once" when it's up and running. Blue Origin has invested more than $3 billion in its infrastructure and facilities in Florida, which now spans more than 20 sites across the state's Brevard and Orange counties, with more than 5,000 employees, [Ian Richardson, Blue Origin's senior vice president of operations, wrote in the blog post]. The article notes it's part of "a flurry of investment" as SpaceX stops offering commercial rides on its Falcon 9, "with $92.5 billion invested in the commercial space sector in the first three quarters of 2026, according to a report this week by venture capital firm Space Capital." And it happens as Blue Origin, SpaceX and other rocket providers "are seeing increasing demand from companies and governments trying to deploy satellites into orbit." "Launching at a high cadence requires a connected system," says Blue Origin's blog post, "one that manufactures vehicles at scale, prepares cust
articles.summary: 蓝色起源宣布投入3.3亿美元升级佛罗里达发射设施，新增两个新格伦火箭发射着陆台，目标十年末实现每周多飞。

articles.title: Linux Maintainers Can Now Submit AI-Generated Code Without Declaring It
articles.content: Linux maintainers "have ruled that people no longer have to declare their LLM usage," reports XDA Developers, "as Torvalds himself calls a ban on AI 'utterly stupid.'" The first part of this story comes via a message sent to the Linux mailing list. It announces one of the major changes decided during the Maintainers Summit on October 8, 2026, in Prague, Czechia, where submissions to the kernel no longer need to use the "Assisted-by" tag... meaning that people can submit AI-generated code without needing to declare it as such. In some correspondence regarding concern about this new disclosure removal, the creator of Linux, Linus Torvalds, made his thoughts known... [Torvalds] compares an AI ban to getting rid of text editors, as doing so would prove that someone could write a good commit message without making any mistakes. He then rounds off his argument by asking, "Do you not see how UTTERLY STUPID those kinds of rules would be?" and stating that he simply expects the people working on the Linux kernel to "understand what they are doing." Here's the last line of Torvalds' post. "Quite honestly, in my experience, the people I respect and call intelligent are not the ones that shy away from using new and interesting tools." In a related story, Torvalds says he's used AI to help him understand patches that were hard to follow. And this week Torvalds even posted an LLM-assisted patch, reports Tom's Hardware: The development branch purports to fix an old issue with massive cache contention when many CPUs are reading the same file — a scenario potentially encountered when using shared libraries, databases, and web servers. Several developers had already made attempts over the years at fixing the issue, all with varied results, none quite ideal as an all-encompassing solution... He's now posted his solution in a development branch, and claims that he's seen a 23x performance improvement in a dedicated synthetic benchmark, though he notes that actual real-world impact will

articles.title: Scientists Discover Why Microplastics Trigger Inflammation
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Scientific American: Microplastics are a source of extreme concern for health: the presence of these tiny pieces of plastic has been linked to heart attacks, stroke, dementia and brain tumors. But what drives these associations is unclear. Now a study published in Nature offers a tantalizing clue: microplastics interact with water, generating highly reactive molecules. When microplastics come into contact with water, the water near their surface can become chemically active, generating highly reactive species that can modify nearby substances, including biologically important molecules. As plastics wear down to microscopic sizes, their surface-to-volume ratio increases dramatically. For example, when a credit card is fragmented into particles some 10 microns in diameter, there is a more than 200-fold increase in its surface area, says Wei Min, a chemist at Columbia University and one of the senior authors of the study. As a result, any chemical activity is amplified. Min and his colleagues examined various microplastics -- including polystyrene, polyethylene, polyvinyl chloride, polypropylene and polyethylene terephthalate. Plastic surfaces are hydrophobic, meaning they repel water, Min says. Thus, water molecules cannot form the hydrogen bonds they maintain in liquid form. That changes molecular arrangements, and, in turn, the change influences the local electrical environment and chemical reactivity. The presumed chemical inertness of bulk plastics overlooks the toxicity of their fragmented microscale forms. "For microplastics, this is especially important because fragmentation creates enormous amounts of new surface area," Min says. In past research, microplastics have been shown to cause inflammation, oxidative stress and decreased mitochondrial activity. The new study provides a possible mechanism for this, showing that plastic-water interfaces can perturb proteins, cell membranes, and more. How this might contribute to
